title: A method for quantifying vertical stratification in crude oil emulsions by rotational viscometry
author: Hartyányi, Nagy

steps.title: Prepare emulsion sample
steps.instruction: Formulate the crude‑oil–produced‑water–surfactant emulsion with the desired oil volume fraction (ϕ_oil), aqueous salinity, and surfactant concentration (c_surf); complete emulsification and transfer the bulk sample into the measurement column of height H.

steps.title: Define aging start and store
steps.instruction: Mark the moment after emulsification and transfer as t = 0 min; store the column quiescently at a controlled temperature (e.g., 80 °C) in a jacketed vessel until measurements are taken.

steps.title: Set up Brookfield viscometer
steps.instruction: Install a Brookfield Amatek DVNext rotational viscometer with a helipath spindle appropriate for the expected viscosity range; fix the rotation speed (value kept constant for the whole series); set the measurement temperature to T_meas = 80 °C and verify torque is within the manufacturer‑specified reliable range.

steps.title: Design measurement schedule
steps.instruction: Choose measurement times t_j (j = 1…M) in minutes; use a dense early‑phase sampling to capture rapid stratification onset and a sparser late‑phase sampling for slower changes.

steps.title: Select height positions
steps.instruction: Define N relative height positions z_i* (i = 1…N) across the column (e.g., N = 16 for a full grid); the absolute height is z_i = z_i* × H (cm).

steps.title: Record height‑resolved viscosities
steps.instruction: For each scheduled time t_j, move the spindle sequentially to each height z_i*, record the apparent viscosity η(z_i*,t_j); optionally acquire n technical replicates at each height (e.g., n = 5 for repeatability tests, n = 3 for SI repeatability).

substeps.instruction: Position spindle at the first relative height and record η.
Repeat the whole height scan for each time point t_j.

steps.title: Calculate column‑averaged viscosity
steps.instruction: For each time point t_j compute η̄(t_j) = (1/N) ∑_{i=1}^{N} η(z_i*,t_j).

steps.title: Compute stratification index
steps.instruction: For each time point t_j calculate SI(t_j) = [1/(N η̄(t_j))] ∑_{i=1}^{N} |η(z_i*,t_j) − η̄(t_j)|; note that SI ≥ 0 and SI = 0 indicates a homogeneous profile.

steps.title: Derive kinetic descriptors (optional)
steps.instruction: From the SI(t) curve determine the stratification onset time (t_sep), fit an appropriate kinetic model to obtain a rate constant k and the asymptotic value SI_∞.

steps.title: Validate viscosity repeatability
steps.instruction:
At t = 0 min measure at N = 3 predefined heights with n = 5 technical replicates each; compute mean η, standard deviation, and relative standard deviation (RSD %). Reported results: 
- Height 1: mean η = 1.00 mPa·s, SD = 32.5 mPa·s, RSD = 0.36 % 
- Height 2: mean η = 1.12 mPa·s, SD = 0.53 mPa·s, RSD = 0.48 % 
- Height 3: mean η = 0.99 mPa·s, SD = 0.80 mPa·s, RSD = 2.58 % 
- Height 4: mean η = 0.00 mPa·s, SD = 2.28 mPa·s, RSD = 0.14 % (values taken from Table 1).

steps.title: Validate SI repeatability
steps.instruction:
At t = 0 min and t = 60 min acquire height‑resolved viscosity profiles at N = 16 heights with n = 3 replicates; compute SI for each replicate and summarize: 
- 0 min: mean SI = 0.048, SD = 0.002, RSD = 3.91 % 
- 60 min: mean SI = 0.212, SD = 0.001, RSD = 0.28 % (Table 2).

steps.title: Assess batch‑to‑batch reproducibility
steps.instruction:
Prepare m = 3 independent batches of the same formulation; for each batch record viscosity at N = 16 heights at t = 0 min and t = 60 min; compute SI and summarize: 
- 0 min: mean SI = 0.047, SD = 0.002, RSD = 4.10 % 
- 60 min: mean SI = 0.210, SD = 0.002, RSD = 0.72 % (Table 3).

steps.title: Perform homogeneous null test
steps.instruction: Fill the measurement column with a non‑stratifying reference fluid (brine); measure apparent viscosity at N = 16 heights with n = 3 replicates using the same instrument settings; compute SI_null, which was found to be 0.0002, confirming that non‑zero SI values for emulsions arise from genuine vertical heterogeneity.
